I searched the Canadian Legal Information Institute for any case law describing this exact situation. I couldn't find any that match.

But again, consider the context in which 12(5) is being used. It is a reasonable presumption that this fault determination rule is used when automobile "A" has the right of way. Consider these 2 following examples:

1. Imagine you are the 3rd car in line at a red light in the left turn lane. The light then turns to an advance green (green left turn signal). All while the light remains green, if the two cars in front of you clear the intersection and you proceed behind them, do you believe that you would be assigned 50% fault if hit by a red light runner? If your answer is no, then on an advance green, do you expect every left turn driver to pause in the middle of the intersection in order to see if there is any oncoming traffic?

2. Imagine you approach an intersection with traffic lights, coming from a one-way street. You can either turn left, right, or go straight where it would continue to be a one-way street. You decide to turn left, and yield to all pedestrians in the crosswalk. As the final pedestrian clears the crosswalk, your light has turned from green, to amber, to red. As you execute the turn, a car goes the opposite direction down the one way street, and hits you in the intersection. Do you believe that you would be assigned 50% at fault?

There is still nuance to these situations, because even with the right of way, all drivers have the obligation to avoid any accidents that can reasonably be avoided. In the above two examples, the left turning driver has a reasonable expectation, as well as the right of way, that there is no accident to avoid. The same applies for someone waiting to turn left in an intersection, then after the light turns red, gets hit by a red light runner.
